Blender can composite. With AE everything is done in layers. In Blender align your media along the Z axis and enable "Import Images as Planes" in Preferences. Set the camera pointing at your image planes and you have layers just like in AE. It's a PITA. But the same approach is used for South Park in Maya. And it works well.

Remember: Everything has a keyframe. You'll be spending most of your time in the dopesheet with either program anyway.

Many common AE effects can be done in Blender easily. Titling is very easy and produces professional results. There's mesh deformation, just like the Puppet Pin tool in AE and Photoshop. There's masking and rotoscoping tools, just like in AE. Freestyle will autotrace lines by edge detect, somewhat similar to AE's cartoon effect. There's a complete set of rigging tools for Inverse Kinematics to make 3D puppets which can be used for 2D as well. You'd need an addon in AE for that (but there's a good free one, see Duik by Duduf). Lip syncing can be handled manually or by moho files (see the free tool Papagayo), both with AE using a hack script and in Blender. Otherwise AE requires expensive add-ons. Blender has a range of particle effects like AE. And has physics effects you'd have to buy an expensive add-on to get in AE. And the node editor allows for color correction and grading.

Blender has a full NLE that reasonably compares to early versions of Final Cut Pro. Not quite as nice as Premiere but good enough to get work done. And you can call GIMP script-fu python modules from within Blender, transferring some functionality from GIMP over to Blender.

All in all, Blender reasonably compares with Adobe tools for filmmaking. Though you won't land a job for learning the tool. OTOH: if you want to release a film project legally and can't afford commercial tools, Blender does the job. Even if its interface is a PITA.
